newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Audi seeks record results in 1997.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Audi seeks record results in 1997.

text.p: German luxury carmaker Audi AG, a unit of Volkswagen AG, said on Wednesday it expected to post record sales and earnings in 1997, thanks in part to strong demand for its new A6 saloon.

Audi said at its annual general meeting that it expected 1997 sales to top 20 billion marks ($11.6 billion) compared with 18.8 billion marks in 1996 and to report a higher pre-tax profit than the 1996 level of 862 million marks.

Audi, also noting strong demand for its A3 compact, said it expected to sell more than 500,000 cars during the year, up from 492,000 last year, and for final first-half sales to rise 16 percent to 10.8 billion marks.

Franz-Josef Paefgen, who took over as Audi management board chairman at the meeting, said global vehicle sales during the first half of the year were up 12.9 percent to 277,000 units. Paefgen replaces Herbert Demel, who will head VW's Brazil unit.
But Audi, noting its production capacity was fully utilised, said it expected slower sales growth in the second half of the year compared with the first half.
Audi also came under criticism from some of the remaining individual shareholders about its dividend policy, with one saying VW was plundering the carmaker at their expense.
The carmaker, which is 99 percent owned by VW, paid a 1996 dividend of nine marks per share, up from six marks in 1995.
Audi, which had a 1996 pre-tax profit of 862 million marks, said it would transfer 125 million marks to VW in 1996, up from 80 million marks in 1995.

Despite the criticism, Audi's domestic sales have been surging. Sales in Germany were up 11.7 percent during the six-month period, which boosted Audi's domestic market share at the end of May to seven percent from 5.8 percent in April.

In western Europe outside of Germany, sales were up 12.3 percent during the first half of the year. Sales in the United States rose about 30 percent and Japanese sales were up 18.1 percent, the carmaker said.
Audi's workforce at the end of June was up almost 10 percent over the level in June 1996, rising by about 3,400 workers to 37,400.
The carmaker said it was reviewing programmes on how its employees could participate financially in its performance.
Audi management board member Andreas Schleef said possible programmes were under discussion that would reward employees based on sales, quality, productivity and number of sick days.
The carmaker was also reviewing the terms of a similar programme recently announced by VW. Schleef did not say when any such programme would begin at Audi.
